rationale: A wins because it finds the harder, more usable press line: "Liquid Death says it's profitable. It just won't say by how much." That is a real business-reporter angle hiding in the update, and B leaves it in the penalty box as a warning instead of turning it into a pitchable scrutiny story. B is cleaner in places, but "Liquid Death's first store sells T-shirts, limited-run cans and event tickets — not a new product" soft-invents details and lands less sharply.
gaps_in_A: "Liquid Death's new store sells water you can't buy anywhere else — for now" overclaims exclusivity; the update only says the store sells limited-edition canned water, not that it is store-exclusive.
"the limited-edition can launches alongside the store opening" adds launch timing that was not supplied.
The beverage-trade angle is the weakest kept angle; without proof that the can differs from normal SKUs or is a real distribution test, it is a merch-drop curiosity.
"confirmation of whether net profit has ever been modeled internally" is oddly speculative proof; the cleaner ask is net profit, gross-to-net bridge, or contribution-margin methodology.
gaps_in_B: "event tickets" is invented; the facts say the store runs in-store events, not that it sells tickets.
"T-shirts" is needlessly specific; the update says merch, and guessing the merch item is how small hallucinations sneak into otherwise competent work.

It misses the best contrarian angle: contribution-margin profitability with no net profit disclosure. The refused "proving challenger beverage brands can win" version is bad, but the underlying finance scrutiny is good.
"category-creation" is the wrong label for the second angle; this is experiential retail or brand/merch strategy, not a category-creation story.
